question_text: An FM integration unexpectedly returns incomplete or truncated responses. Context window diagnostic logs show inputs near the model's maximum token limit. Which remediation approaches are correct? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Use dynamic chunking to limit conversation history size passed to the FM
Redesign the prompt to use summarised conversation history rather than full raw history
Increase the max output tokens to compensate for input truncation
Use a larger FM so it has more parameters to handle long inputs
Add more detail to the system prompt to guide the FM on long inputs

explanation: Skill 5.2.1 describes context window overflow diagnostics, dynamic chunking strategies, and prompt design optimisation. (A) Dynamic chunking limits how many history tokens are included in the context window at any time. (B) Summarising conversation history compresses many tokens of history into a small summary, freeing context space. Increasing max output tokens doesn't affect the input token limit. A larger FM doesn't have a larger context window by default. Adding more to the system prompt worsens the overflow.

question_text: A Lambda function calling Bedrock frequently returns `ValidationException: Input is too long for requested model`. What is the correct debugging workflow?

options.text: Increase Lambda memory
Log the input token count before each API call, identify which inputs exceed the model's context limit, and apply input truncation or chunking
Ignore the error — it is intermittent and will self-resolve
Switch to a different AWS region where the limit may be higher

explanation: Skill 5.2.2 describes error logging and request validation for FM integration issues. The correct approach is: instrument the input with a token counter, log it to CloudWatch, identify inputs that breach the model limit, and apply remediation (truncation, summarisation, chunking). Lambda memory doesn't affect the FM's token limit. ValidationException errors are deterministic — they won't self-resolve without code changes. The context limit is a model property, not a region configuration.
source_topic: FM API errors, ValidationException, token limit

question_text: FM responses to a customer-facing assistant have degraded — answers are suddenly verbose and off-topic. The application code has not changed. A new prompt template was deployed yesterday. Which debugging approach is most systematic?

options.text: Roll back the entire application to last month's deployment
Use Bedrock Prompt Management version comparison — A/B test the previous and new prompt templates against a golden question set and compare output quality metrics
Increase FM temperature to generate more varied responses
Switch to a different FM provider

explanation: Skill 5.2.3 describes prompt testing frameworks and version comparison for prompt engineering issues. Bedrock Prompt Management retains versioned templates; comparing the current version against the previous one on a golden question set isolates the prompt change as the root cause. Rolling back the full application is overly broad and loses new features. Increasing temperature worsens inconsistency. Switching FM providers doesn't fix a prompt regression.
source_topic: Prompt versioning, A/B testing, Bedrock Prompt Management

question_text: Users report that the RAG assistant gives correct answers to some questions but completely ignores relevant documents for others. How should the team diagnose the retrieval failure?

options.text: Assume the FM is hallucinating and increase the top-k retrieval count

Inspect retrieval logs: check embedding quality for failing queries, examine cosine similarity scores for retrieved chunks, and verify that relevant documents are present and properly chunked in the index
Switch to a larger FM — retrieval issues are always generation problems
Delete and rebuild the knowledge base from scratch

explanation: Skill 5.2.4 describes retrieval system troubleshooting including embedding quality diagnostics, drift monitoring, and vectorisation issue resolution. The correct systematic approach: check if relevant documents exist in the index; verify their chunks are appropriately sized; inspect similarity scores for failing queries (low scores indicate embedding mismatch); check for embedding quality drift if a model was recently updated. Increasing top-k may mask the problem. Retrieval failures are distinct from generation — switching FM won't fix a missing-document issue. Full rebuilds are disruptive and don't diagnose root cause.

topic: Prompt maintenance with CloudWatch and X-Ray
question_text: A production FM assistant started producing inconsistent responses after a prompt template variable was added. The CloudWatch Logs show some prompts fail schema validation. Which tools and approach diagnose and fix the issue? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query prompt invocation logs and identify which template variable substitutions are missing or malformed
Use AWS X-Ray to trace the prompt construction path through the application and identify where variables are missing
Increase Lambda memory to resolve template substitution failures
Use Amazon Rekognition to detect problems in prompt text
Use Amazon Macie to scan prompts for PII causing failures

explanation: Skill 5.2.5 explicitly cites CloudWatch Logs to diagnose prompt confusion and X-Ray to implement prompt observability pipelines, alongside schema validation for format inconsistencies. (A) CloudWatch Logs Insights can filter invocations where variable substitution was incomplete — showing the malformed prompt. (B) X-Ray traces the full request path, pinpointing which Lambda function or step lost the variable value. Lambda memory has no effect on template logic. Rekognition is for image/video. Macie detects PII, not template syntax errors.
source_topic: CloudWatch Logs Insights, X-Ray, prompt observability

topic: Embedding model version drift — RAG silent failure
question_text: A financial services RAG application worked correctly for months. After a Lambda code update, it returns 'no relevant information found' for queries that previously retrieved accurate results. CloudWatch shows no errors, X-Ray confirms successful FM invocations, and OpenSearch is healthy with no index changes. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The Lambda IAM role is missing bedrock:InvokeModel permission
The FM temperature was inadvertently increased in the code update
The document vectors in OpenSearch were deleted during the deployment
The Lambda code update switched to a different embedding model version, creating a vector-space mismatch with the existing index

explanation: Skill 5.2.4 (retrieval system troubleshooting) describes embedding model version drift as a classic silent RAG failure. If the Lambda now embeds queries using model v2 while the OpenSearch index contains vectors from model v1, the two vector spaces are mathematically incompatible — no vectors match, retrieval returns zero results. The key diagnostic clue is 'silent failure': no errors (IAM permission errors produce AccessDeniedException logs; deleted indices produce empty-results warnings with different signatures). The FM temperature (B) only affects generation step 2 — retrieval failure happens in step 1 before generation. Vector deletion (C) would normally produce warnings.
source_topic: Embedding drift, vector-space mismatch, RAG troubleshooting

topic: KB ingestion logging for document-level failures
question_text: A company ingests 2,000 documents per day into a Bedrock Knowledge Base from S3. Some documents fail silently — they appear processed but queries return no results for their content. The team needs to identify which specific documents failed and why. Which solution provides document-level ingestion diagnostics?

options.text: Enable Knowledge Base logging to CloudWatch Logs; use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query per-document status codes (SUCCESS / EMBEDDING_FAILED / INDEXING_FAILED)
Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for all Bedrock APIs
Enable Bedrock Model Invocation Logging to capture embedding metrics
Use Amazon CloudWatch Application Signals to detect KB performance issues

explanation: Skill 5.2.4 and 4.3.2 describe Knowledge Base logging for ingestion troubleshooting. The KB-specific logging feature emits per-document status records to CloudWatch Logs (RESOURCE_IGNORED, EMBEDDING_FAILED, INDEXING_FAILED, SUCCESS) that can be queried with Logs Insights. CloudTrail (B) records which IAM principal called StartIngestionJob — it has no visibility into per-document processing outcomes. Bedrock Model Invocation Logging (C) captures prompt/response content during chat inference — unrelated to the background ingestion process. CloudWatch Application Signals (D) is APM for microservices (EKS/API Gateway latency) — not for KB ingestion diagnostics.
source_topic: Bedrock Knowledge Base logging, CloudWatch Logs Insights

question_text: During a high-traffic product launch, a Bedrock-powered chatbot begins returning ThrottlingException errors. The on-call engineer needs to resolve the issue quickly. Which combination of actions is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Implement exponential backoff with jitter in the client so retries do not cause a retry storm
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model to guarantee sustained invocation capacity
Reduce the model temperature to stop throttling
Switch to a larger context window size to avoid the quota
Disable all guardrails to reduce latency overhead

explanation: ThrottlingException indicates the invocation rate has exceeded the on-demand quota. Exponential backoff with jitter (option A) is the standard immediate mitigation — it spreads retries over time and prevents a retry storm. Provisioned Throughput (option B) is the long-term fix: it reserves dedicated model capacity ensuring sustained throughput. Lowering temperature, using a larger context window, or disabling guardrails do not affect throttling quotas.
source_topic: Throttling, Provisioned Throughput, exponential backoff, quota management

topic: Amazon Polly — text-to-speech in GenAI pipeline
question_text: A GenAI virtual assistant generates text responses. The team wants to add voice output so users can listen to answers on a mobile app. Which AWS service converts the FM-generated text to natural-sounding speech?

options.text: Amazon Polly — converts text to lifelike speech, supporting multiple languages and neural voices
Amazon Transcribe — converts speech to text (the opposite direction)
Amazon Lex — builds conversational interfaces but does not output audio directly
Amazon Rekognition — analyzes audio and video content

explanation: Amazon Polly is AWS's text-to-speech service, producing lifelike audio from text in dozens of languages using standard and neural voices. Transcribe is speech-to-text (the reverse). Lex builds conversational AI chatbots and does use Polly under the hood, but Lex itself is not directly invoked for text-to-speech synthesis in a custom pipeline. Rekognition analyzes visual media — not audio synthesis.
source_topic: Amazon Polly, text-to-speech, GenAI voice interface

topic: Amazon Athena — querying S3 data lakes for GenAI evaluation
question_text: A team stores FM invocation logs and evaluation metrics in Amazon S3 in Parquet format. They want to run ad-hoc SQL queries against this data to identify patterns in hallucinations and latency spikes without loading data into a database. Which service enables serverless SQL directly on S3?

options.text: Amazon Athena — runs serverless SQL queries directly on S3 data using standard SQL, with no data movement or ETL
Amazon Redshift — requires loading data into a managed warehouse first
Amazon DynamoDB — a NoSQL key-value store that does not support SQL
Amazon RDS — a relational database requiring data migration from S3

explanation: Amazon Athena is a serverless interactive query service that runs SQL directly on data in S3 (Parquet, CSV, JSON, ORC, etc.) with no ETL or data loading required. This is ideal for ad-hoc analysis of FM invocation logs. Redshift requires loading data into a warehouse. DynamoDB is NoSQL. RDS requires migration from S3.
source_topic: Amazon Athena, serverless SQL on S3, GenAI observability

topic: Amazon QuickSight — BI dashboards for GenAI metrics
question_text: A GenAI platform team wants to build visual dashboards showing token usage trends, cost per team, and guardrail trigger rates over time, accessible to non-technical stakeholders. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?

options.text: Amazon QuickSight — a serverless BI service for building interactive dashboards from AWS data sources including Athena, S3, and CloudWatch
Amazon CloudWatch — provides metrics and alarms but is not a BI dashboarding tool for business stakeholders
AWS Cost Explorer — shows cost trends but cannot be customized for GenAI-specific metrics like guardrail triggers
Amazon SageMaker Studio — a development IDE, not a BI dashboard platform

explanation: Amazon QuickSight is AWS's managed BI service, enabling rich visual dashboards for business stakeholders with no infrastructure to manage. It connects to Athena, S3, CloudWatch, RDS, and more, making it suitable for GenAI usage analytics. CloudWatch is operational monitoring (not stakeholder-facing BI). Cost Explorer is limited to billing dimensions. SageMaker Studio is a data science IDE.
source_topic: Amazon QuickSight, BI dashboards, GenAI metrics visualization
